args.body:
REDLINE REVIEW MEMORANDUM
Concession Agreement — TxDOT Counterparty Markup
Matter: Energy / Natural Resources — Analyze Counterparty Markup of Concession Agreement
Deliverable: redline-review-memorandum.docx
Classification: Privileged and Confidential — Attorney Work Product

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

This memorandum compares the TxDOT (counterparty) markup of the Concession Agreement against our original draft and negotiation playbook, cross-referenced to lender and surety side letters and the project financial model. We reconcile every identified deviation against the base materials, disclosure schedules, and Exhibit B survival matrix. Controlling client instruction (latest partner email): the client will concede conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket, but treats any reduction in the survival period for core representations as a walk-away issue. Earlier messages stating the opposite priority ordering are superseded and are not followed.

Three material deviations require action:

  1. Indemnification economics — silent reduction of the indemnification cap; basket converted from deductible to tipping basket.
  2. Material Adverse Effect (MAE) — new carve-outs for regulatory action of the type already at issue and disclosed on Schedule 3.7.
  3. Survival / limitation period — shortened survival for core representations, contradicting Exhibit B.

Overall risk posture: HIGH on survival and MAE; MODERATE on indemnification cap (basket conversion is client-authorized to concede). Recommended posture: accept basket conversion only; restore cap; reject MAE regulatory carve-outs as drafted; reject survival reduction as a walk-away issue and reinstate Exhibit B matrix.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
II. MATERIALS REVIEWED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Base / firm materials
  • Original draft Concession Agreement (firm-standard energy/natural-resources form)
  • Negotiation playbook (indemnity, MAE, and survival positions)
  • Lender side letter(s) and surety letter(s) (financing and performance-security constraints)
  • Project financial model (indemnity headroom, reserve, and DSCR sensitivity)

Counterparty paper
  • TxDOT markup of the Concession Agreement

Disclosure architecture (controls over general base statements)
  • Schedule 3.7 — two pending regulatory inquiries intersecting the markup’s MAE carve-outs
  • Schedule 5.2 — retained liabilities that the markup’s indemnification changes would silently shift
  • Exhibit B — survival matrix contradicted by the markup’s limitation-period change

Deal-team instruction
  • Latest partner email: concede basket conversion; survival-period reduction is walk-away
  • Misfiled unrelated correspondence in the matter folder was identified and is not relied upon

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
III. METHODOLOGY AND RISK-RATING KEY
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Each deviation is assessed for (a) delta from original draft / playbook, (b) interaction with Schedules 3.7 and 5.2 and Exhibit B, (c) consistency with lender and surety requirements, (d) financial-model impact, and (e) client walk-away / concede guidance.

Risk ratings:
  • CRITICAL — walk-away or financing/surety break; do not accept without structural cure
  • HIGH — material value transfer or closing/condition risk; counter firmly
  • MODERATE — negotiable within playbook bands; accept only with compensating terms
  • LOW — stylistic or non-economic; accept or lightly revise

Disposition labels used below: ACCEPT / ACCEPT WITH MODIFICATION / REJECT / WALK-AWAY.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
IV. DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION ANALYSIS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 1 — Indemnification Cap Reduction and Basket Conversion
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup change
  TxDOT’s revision (i) silently reduces the indemnification cap below the level in our original draft and (ii) converts the indemnification basket from a deductible (true deductible; amounts below the basket are never recoverable) to a tipping basket (once the threshold is exceeded, losses are recoverable from the first dollar).

B. Original draft / negotiation playbook
  • Cap: firm playbook sets the general indemnification cap at the negotiated reference level tied to concession value / fee budget and consistent with lender loss-recovery expectations (typically a defined percentage of aggregate concession consideration or a fixed dollar ceiling cross-referenced in the financing package). Silent reductions are outside playbook authority.
  • Basket: original draft uses a deductible basket. Playbook preference is deductible; tipping basket is a known concession lever that may be traded for preservation of cap, survival, and fundamental-rep carve-outs from the basket/cap.

C. Schedule and exhibit cross-reference
  • Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. A reduced cap plus a tipping basket changes the economic allocation of those retained items: tipping increases first-dollar exposure once the threshold is hit, while a lower cap truncates recovery on large Schedule 5.2-type losses. The markup would silently shift residual risk associated with scheduled retained liabilities onto our client unless the cap is restored and Schedule 5.2 items are treated as retained (or as fundamental / excluded from cap, as applicable under the draft).
  • Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials; any indemnity rewrite must expressly preserve Schedule 5.2 allocation.

D. Lender and surety cross-reference
  • Lender letters typically require that sponsor/concessionaire indemnity and recovery rights remain sufficient to support projected cash flows and cure rights. A silent cap reduction can impair the loss-recovery assumption embedded in the financing case and may require lender consent or a bring-down of the side letter.
  • Surety letters size performance and payment security off expected claim and indemnity profiles. Reducing the counterparty’s indemnity cap without a corresponding adjustment to security or reserves creates a gap between contractual recovery and surety exposure.

E. Financial model
  • Model indemnity headroom and contingency reserves assume the original cap. A lower cap increases unrecoverable tail loss and can pressure DSCR / lock-up metrics if a Schedule 5.2-scale liability crystallizes.
  • Tipping vs. deductible: tipping is modestly adverse on expected loss (first-dollar recovery after tip) relative to deductible, but client has authorized this concession. Model impact of tipping alone is secondary to cap integrity.

F. Client instruction
  • Basket conversion (deductible → tipping): CONCEDE.
  • Cap reduction: not authorized; treat as a separate economic give that must be restored or compensated.

G. Risk rating
  • Cap reduction: HIGH
  • Basket conversion: MODERATE (client-authorized concede)

H. Disposition
  • Basket conversion: ACCEPT
  • Cap reduction: REJECT — restore original cap

I. Counter-proposal language
  “Section [Indemnification — Limitations]. The aggregate liability of [Concessionaire/Indemnifying Party] for indemnifiable Losses under Section [__], other than Losses arising from [Fundamental Representations], fraud, willful misconduct, or matters set forth on Schedule 5.2 as retained by [Counterparty], shall not exceed the Cap Amount equal to $[ORIGINAL CAP] (or [__]% of the aggregate Concession Value), which Cap Amount shall not be reduced except by written agreement of the Parties with prior written confirmation that such reduction is permitted under the Financing Documents and any Surety Instruments.

  The Basket shall be a tipping basket in the amount of $[BASKET]. From and after the time aggregate indemnifiable Losses exceed the Basket, the Indemnifying Party shall be liable for the full amount of such Losses from the first dollar (subject to the Cap Amount and any express exclusions). For the avoidance of doubt, (i) Losses arising from Fundamental Representations, fraud, willful misconduct, and Schedule 5.2 retained-liability true-ups shall neither count toward nor be limited by the Basket or the Cap Amount, and (ii) nothing in this Section modifies the allocation of retained liabilities set forth on Schedule 5.2.”

J. Negotiation note
  Trade acknowledgment of tipping basket expressly against restoration of the original cap and against any attempt to pull Schedule 5.2 items under the reduced ceiling. Require express “no silent amendment” language so that cap figures in schedules, term sheets, and financing abstracts remain aligned.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 2 — Material Adverse Effect Definition — Regulatory-Action Carve-Outs
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup change
  TxDOT adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action “of exactly the kind at issue in this matter,” narrowing the events that can constitute an MAE (and thereby narrowing walk-away, condition-to-closing, and related termination/indemnity triggers).

B. Original draft / negotiation playbook
  • Playbook MAE is standard long-form: material adverse effect on business, assets, liabilities, operations, condition (financial or otherwise), or ability to perform under the Concession Agreement, with limited customary carve-outs (general economic, industry-wide, market, and law changes applying generally), often with “disproportionate impact” exceptions back into MAE.
  • Playbook does not accept carve-outs that eliminate regulatory actions that are company-specific, enforcement-specific, or already teed up in diligence — especially where disclosed inquiries exist.

C. Schedule and exhibit cross-reference
  • Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup’s MAE carve-outs. If regulatory action of that kind is carved out of MAE, the very risk profile the schedule flags becomes incapable of supporting an MAE-based condition, termination right, or related remedy — even if an inquiry ripens into a material order, fine, permit restriction, or operating limitation.
  • Under the controlling principle that scheduled exceptions qualify the base materials, Schedule 3.7 must narrow representations and inform risk allocation; it must not be used by the counterparty as a back-door to erase MAE coverage for the scheduled subject matter. The deliverable reconciles both sources: disclosure of the inquiries stands, and MAE must remain capable of being triggered if those inquiries (or like regulatory actions) become materially adverse.

D. Lender and surety cross-reference
  • Lender MAE / material-adverse-change draw-stop and default constructs often mirror or reference the project-level MAE. Carving out the live regulatory fact pattern can create daylight between the Concession Agreement MAE and financing MAC, complicating enforcement and waiver strategy.
  • Surety underwriting of performance risk assumes that material regulatory impairment remains a recognized adverse event in the contract stack. Broad regulatory carve-outs weaken the contractual recognition of that impairment path.

E. Financial model
  • Model downside cases include regulatory delay, permit constraint, and enforcement-cost scenarios tied to the known inquiry profile. If MAE/condition rights are hollowed out for those paths, the contractual toolset no longer matches the model’s risk cases (price chips, delay damages, or exit rights may be unavailable when the model assumes optionality).

F. Client instruction
  • No client authorization to concede MAE regulatory carve-outs. Not a basket-style give.

G. Risk rating
  • HIGH (approaching CRITICAL if carve-out text is read to blanket-exclude the Schedule 3.7 subject matter from MAE entirely)

H. Disposition
  • REJECT as drafted
  • ACCEPT WITH MODIFICATION only if carve-outs are limited to generally applicable changes in law/regulation with a disproportionate-impact write-back, and expressly do not exclude enforcement actions, orders, penalties, permit denials/revocations, or adverse resolutions arising from the Schedule 3.7 inquiries or any company-specific proceeding

I. Counter-proposal language
  “Material Adverse Effect” means any change, event, effect, state of facts, or occurrence that, individually or in the aggregate, has had or would reasonably be expected to have a material adverse effect on (a) the business, assets, liabilities, operations, reserves, condition (financial or otherwise), or results of operations of the [Project/Concessionaire], (b) the ability of [Party] to perform its obligations under this Agreement or the Financing Documents, or (c) the validity or enforceability of this Agreement or the rights and remedies of [Protected Party] hereunder; provided, however, that none of the following shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur:
    (i) changes in general economic, financial market, or geopolitical conditions;
    (ii) changes generally affecting the industry in which the Project operates;
    (iii) changes in generally applicable Laws or accounting standards, in each case after the date hereof;
  except, in the case of clauses (i)–(iii), to the extent such change, event, effect, state of facts, or occurrence has a disproportionate adverse effect on the [Project/Concessionaire] relative to other similarly situated participants in the same industry, in which case the incremental disproportionate impact may be considered.

  For the avoidance of doubt, none of the following shall be excluded from Material Adverse Effect by reason of any regulatory carve-out: (A) any investigation, inquiry, enforcement action, consent order, penalty, fine, sanction, or directive by a Governmental Authority relating to the Project or [Concessionaire]; (B) any adverse development in respect of the matters disclosed on Schedule 3.7 (including the two pending regulatory inquiries described thereon) or any matter of the same or similar kind; (C) any denial, revocation, suspension, material modification, or non-renewal of a material Permit; and (D) any company-specific regulatory action as distinguished from a generally applicable change in Law.”

J. Negotiation note
  Do not accept a formulation that defines away “regulatory action of the kind at issue.” Insist on Schedule 3.7 express preservation. If TxDOT demands comfort on industry-wide rulemaking, confine it to clause (iii) plus disproportionate-impact write-back. Flag for financing counsel to confirm parallel MAC language in the credit suite.

───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DEVIATION 3 — Survival / Limitation Period — Shortened Survival for Core Representations
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

A. Markup change
  TxDOT introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations below the periods set in our draft and in Exhibit B.

B. Original draft / negotiation playbook
  • Core / fundamental representations (organization, authority, capitalization/ownership as applicable, enforceability, no-conflict as to organic documents, brokers, and other playbook “fundamentals”) survive for a long-stop or statute-of-limitations-plus period.
  • General business representations survive for a defined medium term (playbook band).
  • Certain specials (tax, environmental, employee benefits, as applicable to the concession) survive for their specific statutory or playbook periods.
  • Playbook treats compression of core-rep survival as a structural risk allocation change, not a routine timing tweak.

C. Schedule and exhibit cross-reference
  • Exhibit B sets the survival matrix. The markup’s limitation-period change contradicts Exhibit B. Under the matter’s controlling instruction, scheduled/exhibit exceptions control over general statements; Exhibit B therefore governs unless expressly amended by bilateral agreement with conforming edits to the matrix.
  • Any accepted change must be effected by restating Exhibit B in full (not by a silent general limitation clause that conflicts with the exhibit).

D. Lender and surety cross-reference
  • Lenders rely on post-closing survival and indemnity windows to cover representation breaches that surface after funding or after key drawdowns. Shortening core-rep survival can breach financing representations or require amendments to the lender side letter and intercreditor/direct-agreement package.
  • Sureties evaluate latent-defect and post-completion claim windows partly by reference to contractual survival. Compression may drive increased bonding cost or additional indemnity to the surety.

E. Financial model
  • Tail-risk and escrow/holdback sizing in the model assumes Exhibit B durations. Shorter core-rep survival reduces expected recovery on late-discovered fundamental breaches and may require re-sizing of reserves, contingency, or R&W-type credit support if used.
